item.content:encoded:
The Athletics’ spoiler magic ran out last week, as the team dropped all six games of its final road trip against the first-place Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays. Tonight, the A’s open the last week of the season with the first of two matchups against the Los Angeles Angels, with both teams trying to avoid finishing at the bottom of the American League West standings.
Additionally, with a looming offseason lockout leaving the fate of the 2027 season up in the air, this week may mark the end of the Athletics’ time in Sacramento, which served as a placeholder while their new stadium in Las Vegas gets built. All the more reason for the A’s to try to close out 2026 with a winning homestand.
Roster Move
Before the game, the A’s made a roster move.
Rookie infielder Joshua Kuroda-Grauer has recovered from a ruptured testicle to rejoin the Athletics for the remainder of the season. He spent the past few days on a rehab assignment with the franchise’s Triple-A affiliate, the Las Vegas Aviators, who begin their quest for the Pacific Coast League championship today.
To make room for him, fellow infielder Max Muncy lands on the injured list with left knee chondromalacia, also known as runner’s knee. Additionally, J.T. Ginn, who was shut down for the season a couple of weeks ago, moves to the 60-day injured list.
Game Preview
Back to the game, left-hander Brady Basso will get the A’s final homestand underway. The 28-year-old enters his 25th appearance and seventh opener assignment of the season with a 1-3 record, a 4.50 ERA, a 1.48 WHIP and 28 strikeouts in 40 innings.
Tonight will be Basso’s third consecutive outing as his team’s opener. Two starts ago, he pitched four scoreless innings against the Toronto Blue Jays. However, the southpaw struggled in his most recent outing against the Tampa Bay Rays, allowing four runs on seven hits over 2 2/3 innings.
The A’s will hope Basso pitches as well as he did in his last home game. Yesterday’s off day means the team’s league-worst bullpen is well-rested should Basso’s second career appearance and first start against the Angels only last a couple innings.
Here’s the A’s lineup for the series opener:
At the very least, this lineup should ensure the A’s will be defensively sound, with no players being asked to play out of position. Kuroda-Grauer, who will hopefully remember his cup this time, immediately finds himself in the starting nine at second base. His MLB career was off to a hot start before he suffered the unfortunate injury. Will JKG pick up where he left off, or will he be rusty after spending weeks on the sidelines?
Further down the lineup, center fielder Denzel Clarke receives a rare start to showcase his athleticism on the baseball field. Everyone knows how good a fielder Clarke is, but the jury is still out on whether he will hit enough to warrant a full-time spot on a major league roster. If the A’s want to win, they will need offensive production from Clarke, shortstop Alika Williams and five-hole hitter Tommy White.
The A’s offense will face Angels left-hander Yusei Kikuchi, who is finishing up an injury-plagued campaign. The 35-year-old enters his 13th start of the season with a 1-6 record, a 5.02 ERA, a 1.55 WHIP and 58 strikeouts over 57 1/3 innings.
Tuesday night will be Kikuchi’s first start against the Athletics this season. He has gone 3-5 with a 4.20 ERA and 63 strikeouts in 14 appearances vs. the A’s in his career. Last year, the veteran went 1-2 in three games against the Green and Gold.
And Los Angeles’ starting nine:
The Angels’ lineup quality drops dramatically after Zach Neto and Mike Trout at the top of the order. First baseman Vaughn Grissom has had a solid season, while catcher Moisés Ballesteros was one of the well-known prospects the team acquired during its trade-deadline selloff.
Time to start this final homestand strong and avoid another last-place finish in the division. Let’s go, A’s!

Watch:
Athletics - NBCSCA

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Dodgers Lineup vs. Padres: Andy Pages, Roki Sasaki Are Back
item.dc:creator: Nelson Espinal
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers are opening up for a blockbuster series, their last big test, against the San Diego Padres. Dodgers Lineup 1. Mookie Betts, SS 2. Freddie Freeman, 1B 3. Will Smith, C 4. Max Muncy, 3B 5. Kyle Tucker, RF 6. Teoscar Hernandez, LF 7. Josue De Paula, DH 8. Andy Pages, CF 9. Tommy Edman, 2B Andy Pages is back in the batting order after being activated from the injured list. He broke his hand after getting hit by a pitch, had surgery, and after a month on the shelf, he is back.
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are opening up for a blockbuster series, their last big test, against the San Diego Padres.
Dodgers Lineup
1. Mookie Betts, SS
2. Freddie Freeman, 1B
3. Will Smith, C
4. Max Muncy, 3B
5. Kyle Tucker, RF
6. Teoscar Hernandez, LF
7. Josue De Paula, DH
8. Andy Pages, CF
9. Tommy Edman, 2B
Andy Pages is back in the batting order after being activated from the injured list. He broke his hand after getting hit by a pitch, had surgery, and after a month on the shelf, he is back.
It may take some time for him to shake off the rust at the plate, but his defense should not skip a beat.
The Dodgers are facing righty Michael King, but many of the hottest bats are righties.
Mookie Betts, Will Smith, and Kyle Tucker are among the most dialed-in hitters, and they should drive most of the offense.
Ideally, Freddie Freeman gets going again, since he hasn’t looked right in a while.
Who’s pitching for the Dodgers
The Dodgers will have Brock Stewart as the opener, with Roki Sasaki getting the bulk of the work out of the bullpen.
On Tuesday, hours before the game, Sasaki was activated off the injured list after recovering from his blister.
Sasaki has been great since the All-Star break, posting a 3.05 ERA with 37 strikeouts and 15 walks.
His splitter and slider are fantastic, while the fastball has been the difference-maker, showing some renewed life.
The Japanese righty is set to enter the bullpen in a varied role, either stepping in for a struggling starter or pitching late in high-leverage spots.
Stewart, meanwhile, has been a bit lucky, with a 2.55 ERA and a 3.91 FIP.
FanGraphs’ pitching models have appreciated his stuff and command, and while he has pitched better lately, he is prone to giving up hard contact.

item.title: [whittierdailynews.com] Are the Dodgers finding the best version of themselves just in time?
item.dc:creator: Doug Padilla

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — The energy emanating from the steamroller heading up I-5 on Monday radiated for miles.
Fuel was used to power the buses the San Diego Padres used to make the trip north for a three-game series that starts Tuesday night, but only because they didn’t try adrenaline.
Winners in 13 of their past 14 games, the Padres are poised to accomplish team history over the next few days. Never in their existence have they made the playoffs in three consecutive seasons.
San Diego has a magic number of two to clinch a National League wild-card spot, although the Padres intend to run through the finish line with a chance at ascending to the top of the wild-card heap in the NL.
“I feel like the whole team is in a good spot right now,” San Diego’s Fernando Tatis Jr. told the San Diego Union-Tribune on Sunday. “We’re playing really good baseball. We’re checking in when we have to. The entire lineup is in a good spot right now. So when it’s going like that, it’s … a good time.”
The Dodgers already have another NL West title secured (their 13th in the past 14 years), but they also have a magic number of three to clinch a top-two seed in the NL playoffs and a bye into one of the best-of-five Division Series.
“I think it’s going to be a good kind of (playoff) primer,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said of the upcoming series. “They’re a very talented team. They’re playing as good as anyone in all of baseball. I’m looking forward to playing those guys and just kind of ramping it up a little bit more for our guys.”
With the Dodgers on a 14-3 run since Sept. 3, they are on a familiar final month charge toward the playoffs. Second-half lulls in each of the past two seasons have transformed into Septembers when the group has discovered the best version of itself.
Last season, the Dodgers were swept in a three-game series by the Angels in August then opened September with a three-game dud in Pittsburgh. A disastrous loss in Baltimore lit the fire after Yoshinobu Yamamoto lost a no-hitter with two outs in the ninth inning and the Dodgers never recorded another out while losing the game.
The wide-awake Dodgers went 15-5 the rest of the way, stormed through the NL playoffs – going 9-1 against the Cincinnati Reds, Philadelphia Phillies and Milwaukee Brewers – then came out on top in a dramatic seven-game World Series against the Toronto Blue Jays.
Earlier this month, it was a brutal 8-6 loss in 10 innings to the St. Louis Cardinals on Sept. 2 that was the wake-up call. It included a four-strikeout night from Shohei Ohtani, who played just one more game before taking his current spot on the injured list.
Properly motivated, the Dodgers have gone on a tear ever since, but it has come at the expense of teams that were not in playoff contention like the Washington Nationals, Reds, Miami Marlins and San Francisco Giants.
This week marks the Dodgers’ first chance to face a team playing at the peak of its powers since they faced the Boston Red Sox, Chicago Cubs, Milwaukee Brewers and Atlanta Braves all in a recent 25-game stretch. They flubbed that test by going 1-12 in those games.
Mookie Betts, Kyle Tucker and Will Smith all have put a charge into the resurgence, while the arrival of rookie Josue De Paula has given the lineup another hitter who can extend at-bats with a discerning eye, along with Max Muncy.
Betts went 0 for 4 in Sunday’s 3-1 victory over the Giants, yet he still is hitting .373 with six home runs, 20 RBIs and a 1.215 OPS in 17 games since the start of September.
Far from content with an offense that has averaged 5.8 runs per game this month, Betts said the Dodgers can do even more. After all, Andy Pages is set to return Tuesday, while Ohtani could be back later this week.
“Some guys are hitting, some guys are not,” Betts said. “I think that’s the beauty of the lineup. You get a couple guys going, and a couple guys here can carry a team, and you never know. You just never know who’s it going to be, it’s different guys every day.”
Amid a brutal first season with the Dodgers, Tucker has done his part lately by going 15 for 36 (.417) over his past 11 games with five home runs and 11 RBIs. He was limited to coming off the bench on Sunday after he fouled a ball off his right knee on Saturday.
Tucker was not with the club for last year’s September revival, but he has helped power this one. When it comes to team potential, Tucker is a big-picture guy.
“I think our potential is winning the World Series,” Tucker said. “So (when) we do that, then I can say we reached it. But we feel like we’re in a good spot right now. Our pitching staff’s done a great job all year giving us an opportunity to win every single night. Our defense has played pretty well behind them and then offensively we’ve done a solid job as well.”
“Right now, we got a few guys that are feeling good. A few guys that are banged up. But we’re still out there grinding trying to win as many games as possible before the season ends and just trying to carry it all the way to the playoffs.”
At the very least, confidence will be high this week, in both dugouts.
UP NEXT
Padres (RHP Michael King, 12-9, 3.03 ERA) at Dodgers (TBA), Tuesday, 7:10 p.m., SportsNet LA, 570 AM

item.title: [marinij.com] Wilkinson’s impressive five shutout innings can’t prevent SF Giants from being swept by Dodgers
item.dc:creator: Justice delos Santos
item.description: LOS ANGELES — Matt Wilkinson’s role has been nebulous during his short time in the majors. In his debut, he was an opener. On some days, he’s made traditional starts. In others, he’s been a multi-inning reliever. Wilkinson is one of several young, inexperienced pitchers on this roster trying to prove he can start at the major-league level. His performance on Sunday afternoon at Dodger Stadium helped those efforts. “Tugboat” couldn’t prevent the Giants, who lost 3-1 to the Dodgers, from being swe
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Matt Wilkinson’s role has been nebulous during his short time in the majors. In his debut, he was an opener. On some days, he’s made traditional starts. In others, he’s been a multi-inning reliever.
Wilkinson is one of several young, inexperienced pitchers on this roster trying to prove he can start at the major-league level. His performance on Sunday afternoon at Dodger Stadium helped those efforts.
“Tugboat” couldn’t prevent the Giants, who lost 3-1 to the Dodgers, from being swept, but the rookie turned in arguably the best start of his short career. In his seventh career appearance, Wilkinson tossed five shutout innings against the NL West champions, collecting a career-high six strikeouts without recording a single walk.
“He was outstanding,” said manager Tony Vitello. “Back at it on the starting deal. To be honest with you, didn’t have a whole lot of trouble to navigate because of how well he threw the ball. … When there was potential for things brewing, he put an end to it.”
“Best one yet since being up,” Wilkinson said. “Really was just throwing all four pitches for strikes today, and that was kind of the mindset going into today. Compete with all four pitches, and I felt like I did a good job with that today.”
Vitello said it’s “too early” to know how Wilkinson could fit into next year’s pitching plans but assessed that Wilkinson is “pretty flexible.” Before Sunday, Wilkinson had pitched five scoreless innings with four strikeouts over his last two outings as a multi-inning reliever. When asked if he prefers starting or relieving, the 23-year-old responded he’s willing to pitch whatever role is needed.
“You want a guy that wants the ball and ain’t scared of those situations,” Vitello said.
Wilkinson certainly didn’t look scared in his first meeting with the reigning back-to-back World Series champions on their home turf. Even with Shohei Ohtani on the injured list and Kyle Tucker starting the day on the bench, the Dodgers’ lineup still featured future Hall of Famers Mookie Betts and Freddie Freeman and multi-time All-Stars Max Muncy and Teoscar Hernández.
Against Wilkinson, that group couldn’t get anything cooking.
The only threats that the Dodgers posed against Wilkinson were one-out doubles in the second and fifth innings. On both occasions, Wilkinson maneuvered out of trouble and completed five innings for just the second time in his career.
“Especially with this rivalry, it’s awesome and fun to be a small piece of that,” Wilkinson said.
Despite Wilkinson’s efforts, the Dodgers generated enough offense after his departure to complete the dusting.
Tommy Edman tied the game in the bottom of the sixth by turning a 2-2 cutter from Carson Seymour into a solo homer, and Kiké Hernández drove in the go-ahead run in the bottom of the seventh. Muncy, a long-time Giants (64-92) foe, added an RBI single in the bottom of the eighth for insurance.
Jonah Cox, with the use of his elite speed, generated San Francisco’s lone run in the top of the first.
Cox began the afternoon with a leadoff walk, then scrambled to second when the Dodgers’ Jack Dreyer made an errant pickoff throw. Already in scoring position, Cox swiped third with ease, his 14th steal of the season, then scored on a single by Victor Bericoto.
Following Dreyer’s lone inning as the opener, San Francisco couldn’t generate any offense against Los Angeles’ Emmet Sheehan, who allowed one hit over 5 1/3 scoreless innings of long relief with nine strikeouts. Sheehan has been outstanding against the Giants in his career, allowing four runs over 33 1/3 innings
By afternoon’s end, the Giants were reduced to their most inexperienced, anonymous lineup of the season. Rookie Bryce Eldridge missed a third straight game due to a head laceration, and right fielder Jung Hoo Lee was lifted from the game after fouling a pitch off his groin in the top of the sixth. Eldridge is not expected to play on Monday.
Up next
The Giants will return to Oracle Park for their final six games of the regular season, beginning with a three-game set against the Minnesota Twins.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Dodgers playoff roster projection: Could Edwin Díaz, Josue De Paula, even Hyeseong Kim surprise?
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris

item.content:encoded:
Entering the final week of the regular season, the Dodgers more or less know their postseason fate.
They've locked up the National League West. They are a seemingly safe four games clear of the Atlanta Braves for a first-round bye. And, unless they can close a two-game gap on the Milwaukee Brewers without holding the tiebreaker, they will finish as the NL's No. 2 seed, getting home-field advantage at least for the NL Division Series.
Thus, the real intrigue for now is who might be on the Dodgers' postseason roster when the playoffs begin next month.
This year, injuries and fluctuating performances have forced them to cycle 53 different players through their clubhouse.
And while the core of the group is clear, many questions remain about how the club will construct its lineup and pitching staff for this fall's pursuit of a third-straight World Series.
Here is the California Post's best guess about how it will all shake out.
Lineup locks
Will Smith, Freddie Freeman, Tommy Edman, Mookie Betts, Max Muncy, Teoscar Hernández, Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, Shohei Ohtani, Kiké Hernández, Miguel Rojas, Hunter Feduccia
There won't be any big surprises in how the Dodgers line up to begin the playoffs, assuming Ohtani is healthy enough to resume everyday DH'ing duties.
Teoscar Hernández and Kyle Tucker have cemented their place as everyday hitters thanks to late-season surges. Andy Pages is due back on Tuesday from a fractured hand. Freddie Freeman still seems somewhat limited by his right knee injury, but has nonetheless been able to manage it well enough to this point. And while Tommy Edman has been slumping lately, he doesn't seem to be in immediate danger of losing at-bats.
On the bench, Hunter Feduccia has locked up the back-up catching job, and could be a left-handed hitting option as a pinch-hitter. Kiké Hernández and Miguel Rojas, meanwhile, each provide versatile defensive depth, as well as extensive track records for postseason heroics when called upon.
Entering the final week of the regular season, the core of the Dodgers' position player group looks as they expected.
Dodgers Lineup questions
Bubble candidates: Josue De Paula, Dalton Rushing, Alex Call, Alex Freeland, Hyeseong Kim
The Dodgers will still have one, if not two, position player spots to fill depending on how they construct their roster (i.e. an even 13 pitchers/13 hitters, or a 12/14 split like they used last year?)
And for those, they could have a number of difficult decisions.
First and foremost: Will Josue De Paula make the playoff roster?
If he does, it will likely be as a left-handed bench bat; though if there is any lingering uncertainty with Ohtani, he could also provide insurance as a backup DH option. His main competition right now figures to be Alex Call (who might be redundant to Rojas and Hernández as a right-handed bench bat) or Dalton Rushing (who is an intriguing alternative as a left-handed bat, but remains sidelined from the setback he suffered with his elbow injury earlier this month).
In just 10 MLB games, De Paula has quickly built a strong case, showing supreme plate discipline (10 walks to only four strikeouts) and the potential for power (three doubles, one home run, seven RBIs). At this point, it might be more of a surprise if he doesn't make it.
If the Dodgers elect to carry an extra position player on top of that, the choices are even more varied.
Last year, they rostered two base-running/defensive specialists throughout the playoffs in infielder Hyeseong Kim and outfielder Justin Dean. Dean is now gone, and Hernández could serve as a late-game defensive outfield replacement anyway. But Kim remains in consideration, manager Dave Roberts said, thanks to his speed and infield glove. Alex Freeland could also factor in here, as someone capable of providing more at the plate.
Lineup projection for Los Angeles
C: Will Smith
1B: Freddie Freeman
2B: Tommy Edman
SS: Mookie Betts
3B: Max Muncy
LF: Teoscar Hernández
CF: Andy Pages
RF: Kyle Tucker
DH: Shohei Ohtani
Bench: Kiké Hernández, Miguel Rojas, Hunter Feduccia, Josue De Paula, Hyeseong Kim*
*If the Dodgers carry 14 position players
Dodgers pitching staff locks
Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow, Roki Sasaki, Tanner Scott, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips
The Dodgers' starting rotation is set, assuming no further setbacks with Blake Snell's groin injury. The back end of the bullpen has come into focus, too, with Tanner Scott and/or Roki Sasaki the most logical candidates to serve as closer, and Alex Vesia and Evan Phillips separating themselves as the team's next most-trusted high-leverage relief options.
The only real question here is how the Dodgers will line up the rotation. Yamamoto-Skubal would make sense for Games 1 and 2 of a division series (keeping them both on-line for a potential Game 5). But could Tyler Glasnow's potential issues with traveling tempt the Dodgers to use him primarily at home, if they can? All factors to consider in the coming weeks.
Pitching staff questions
Roster bubble candidates: Brock Stewart, Edwin Díaz, Blake Treinen, Kris Bubic, Jack Dreyer, Emmet Sheehan, Justin Wrobleski, Edgardo Henriquez, Will Klein, Eric Lauer
The first thing the Dodgers need to figure out here is health.
Edgardo Henriquez will almost certainly be on the playoff roster, and pitching in a high-leverage role, if he can make a full recovery from his recent back strain. Will Klein and Eric Lauer might also be available health-wise, though lack clear roles to step immediately back into.
Otherwise, the Dodgers will effectively have at least four open spots for six to seven other pitchers.
For added right-handed depth, they might be deciding between Brock Stewart (who has been a go-to weapon against right-handed hitters recently), Edwin Díaz (who is trying to salvage his dismal debut season, and did throw a pair of scoreless outings this weekend) and Blake Treinen (who has curiously pitched only five times in three weeks since being activated from the injured list, and not in the highest of leverage).
For another left-handed option, they could go with Kris Bubic (the trade deadline acquisition who has impressed with three scoreless appearances since returning from an injury) or Jack Dreyer (who was one of the Dodgers' best relievers from June to August, but has given up five runs in his last seven outings).
And for a multi-inning role, they will have Emmet Sheehan (who has looked like a different pitcher in three sterling starts since returning from a minor-league demotion) and Justin Wrobleski (the breakout All-Star who has finally shaken some of his home run problems since moving to the bullpen).
There are many permutations that the Dodgers could employ depending on opponent. They're still figuring out the exact hierarchy of all their bullpen arms, too.
But as long as their rotation is dominant, everything else should take care of itself.
Pitching staff projection
Rotation: Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow
Bullpen: Roki Sasaki, Tanner Scott, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Kris Bubic, Edwin Díaz, Emmet Sheehan, Justin Wrobleski

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Mookie Betts' sudden revival could be Dodgers' secret weapon in securing three-peat
item.dc:creator: Brandon Glick
item.description: The death of Mookie Betts at the plate appears to have been greatly exaggerated. item.content:encoded:
The death of Mookie Betts at the plate appears to have been greatly exaggerated. The eight-time All-Star certainly won't be able to consider his 2026 campaign alongside some of his historic performances from years past, but he's put together another strong season after a calamitous start.
Specifically since August 17, he's been one of the best hitters in all of baseball. He leads the Los Angeles Dodgers in all three triple-slash categories (.336/.427/.611), wRC+ (183), home runs (seven), RBI (27), and fWAR (2.0) from that point forward, emerging at a time when the team has gotten all of 71 plate appearances (and a 101 wRC+) from Shohei Ohtani.
Betts isn't a "secret weapon" by traditional standards; his MVP credentials and three World Series rings would certainly beg to differ. But after he struggled mightily a year ago and then followed that up with an even worse encore at the beginning of 2026, having him healthy and in his best groove in years could be the deciding factor in the Dodgers' quest for a three-peat.
Mookie Betts has elevated his own floor and with it, the Dodgers' ceiling
The Dodgers are hardly hurting for production, ranking third in the league in runs scored since mid-August. Even without Ohtani, they can batter opposing pitching staffs with their depth, especially now that Kyle Tucker finally looks interested in participating in this group project.
But more than a rejuvenated Tucker or red-hot Teoscar Hernández, there's something special about Betts in particular getting this hot. He's the fourth-longest tenured player on the roster, surpassed by only Max Muncy and Will Smith among position players. He's been around for each of the three recent championships, posting a cumulative OPS over .800 in those playoff runs.
One of the most selfless superstars you'll ever find, there's a "you go, we go" aura that orbits Betts, especially now that he's reclaimed his rightful spot atop the batting order as Dave Roberts' leadoff hitter. His all-around talents lengthen the lineup to a tremendous degree, something opposing pitchers will really feel once Ohtani is back in the fold.
It's not all perfect, of course. His hard-hit rate even during this hot streak is well below the figures he'd post in his prime, and he's still hitting a few too many balls on the ground. Naturally, all of his expected stats during this stretch fall shy of his actual results, including significant disparities in his slugging percentage (.611 compared to a .458 xSLG) and wOBA (.443 compared to a .374 xwOBA).
Those expected metrics are still leaps and bounds better than we got earlier this season, though, and that's the real takeaway here. Even if Betts can't keep this MVP-caliber charade going through all of October, he's clearly found a more stable baseline level of performance that can still help the Dodgers win.

item.title: [fansided.com] MLB Power Rankings: Playoff stakes rise as October contenders make their move
item.dc:creator: Chris Landers; Mark Powell

item.content:encoded:
The playoffs technically don't start for another week or so, but good luck telling that to teams for which every game already feels like October. With the standings in both the NL and AL as jumbled as they've been in recent memory, the stakes are already as high as can be — and whoever gets hot now could well ride that wave all the way to a World Series.
"Hot" could definitely describe both the San Diego Padres and Cleveland Guardians of late. The former has decided to just never lose again, not only grabbing hold of a Wild Card spot but now pushing for home-field in the first round if things break right. The latter, meanwhile, has once again snatched the AL Central while no one was looking. And they're not the only ones making serious moves in our latest MLB power rankings.
But who are we buying as serious title contenders, and who still has work to do? Read on to find out.
30. Colorado Rockies
The Rockies have admittedly let go of the rope of late, well on their way to yet another 100-loss season. There are at least some promising young hitters in this organization, which represents something to build upon moving forward. Of course, the pitching staff remains a mess, and no one's been able to crack that nut yet in Colorado.
–Chris Landers, FanSided.com editor
29. Los Angeles Angels
In Reid Detmers, Walbert Urena and Ryan Johnson, the Angels have at least some sort of foundation upon which to build for the future. Well, OK, maybe not Detmers, who will almost certainly be dealt this offseason. But still, L.A.’s pitching staff has been a real bright spot of late. The offense … well, that’s another question. Things are going to get worse before they get better under John Mozeliak. At least Arte Moreno is no longer around to meddle in it.
–CL
28. Athletics
The A’s are playing out the string of a lost season, although the contributions they’ve gotten from young bats like Henry Bolte, Max Muncy (not that one), Lawrence Butler and Zack Gelof down the stretch have been notable. None of that will matter, though, until the team fixes its pitching staff. We know we sound like a broken record, but it really is that simple, and no potential answers have emerged in the second half.
–CL
27. San Francisco Giants
Rafael Devers' injury, which figures to cost him at least some of next season as well as the end of this one, is a fitting if unfortunate end to what's been a miserable season by the Bay. Devers had been one of the few bright spots on this Giants team down the stretch alongside Bryce Eldridge; now, it's unclear how San Francisco will rebuilt its offense for 2027 in addition to finding reinforcements for a pitching staff that simply hasn't been good enough.
–CL
26. Kansas City Royals
The Kansas City Royals have been eliminated for quite some time now. If there is one clear goal for Kansas City this winter, it's to build a roster around Bobby Witt Jr. that is capable of making a postseason run. That is every team's goal, but the Royals are so far away from contention despite featuring such a prolific player, Witt Jr.'s career is closer to becoming Mike Trout's than Derek Jeter's.
-Mark Powell, FanSided.com MLB director
25. Minnesota Twins
At one point not all that long ago, the Twins had a realistic chance to make the playoffs as the third AL Wild Card spot. Then, the bottom fell out. Byron Buxton underwent successful hip surgery just last week that will keep him out until spring training, whenever that may be. The Twins once again experienced the roster flaw of building around an injured star.
-MP
24. New York Mets
This week couldn’t have been more awkward for the New York Mets when Pete Alonso hit his 300th home run in his return to Citi Field, much to the delight of many Mets fans in attendance, but once Alonso left town, the Mets began to play better, winning two games in a row against the Phillies. Those wins, headlined by more quality play from youngsters like Carson Benge, Zac Thornton and Christian Scott, show why Mets fans should be somewhat enthusiastic for what’s to come.
–Zach Rotman, FanSided.com staff writer
23. Cincinnati Reds
In the American League, the Reds likely wouldn't be the worst team in their division. But the NL Central has been a gauntlet all year long, and the Reds couldn't keep up. Despite breakthrough seasons from Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart, Cincinnati still has a long way to go on the starting pitching front. Can they rely on Hunter Greene and Chase Burns moving forward?
-MP
22. Seattle Mariners
Going 3-3 against the Angels and Rockies this week just about sums up this season in Seattle. The good news is that youngsters like Michael Arroyo and Lazaro Montes have helped to key an offensive turnaround. The bad news is that the starting rotation hasn’t held up its end of the bargain of late, and there are still tons of long-term questions about this lineup — especially with Randy Arozarena set to hit free agency. Jerry DiPoto will need to find some answers this offseason after a year in which just about everything went wrong.
–CL
21. Washington Nationals
The Washington Nationals deserved a better fate in 2026. Even with their offense falling off a bit of late, they’re still third in the majors in runs scored. The dynamic duo of CJ Abrams and James Wood is as good as any in the National League. Recently extended Cade Cavalli is a budding ace. Andrew Alvarez has thrown the ball incredibly well and looks like a future rotation stalwart. If it weren’t for a historically bad bullpen, we’d be talking about this team in Wild Card contention.
–ZR
20. Detroit Tigers
The Tigers have the best run differential in the AL Central and a pythagorean record of an AL playoff team. None of it matters. Scott Harris and the Tigers front office gave up on their team's postseason hopes at the trade deadline. Then, they proceeded to get fans' hopes up with a late August run, only to play like the team Harris assumed they'd become when it mattered most. The Tigers have some work to do, though the emergence of young stars in the lineup like Hao-Yu Lee and Kevin McGonigle, paired with Riley Greene's consistent play, give them some building blocks.
-MP
19. St. Louis Cardinals
The Cardinals are ahead of schedule, but not a postseason team. Make no mistake about it, St. Louis came crashing back down to earth in September, and has been eliminated from playoff contention. There are questions about the long-term future of Masyn Winn, especially with JJ Wetherholt as the de-facto shortstop of the future. But these are all good problems to have. Now, if only Bloom could find an ace burried in that farm system of his.
-MP
18. Baltimore Orioles
A series against league-best Milwaukee came at the worst possible time for the O’s, which now find themselves needing to hit an inside straight to snatch the final Wild Card spot. Pete Alonso’s heroics at Citi Field aside, Baltimore’s bats simply have not been good enough. Heck, no part of this team has; they’re hovering around .500 for a reason, after all, and there’s no reason to think they have the consistency required to get hot over the final week and overtake the White Sox, Blue Jays and Astros.
–CL
17. Miami Marlins
The Miami Marlins tried to do what they could to stick around in the NL postseason hunt, even using Sandy Alcantara on one day of rest in a save opportunity, but they were eliminated following Friday’s loss in San Diego. As disappointing as that is, the Marlins could finish above .500 for just the third time since 2009. That’s a sign that things are heading in the right direction for Miami.
–ZR
16. Toronto Blue Jays
The Jays have lost three of four series now, and news that Dylan Cease will have his next start bumped due to shoulder fatigue makes it even less likely that Toronto can sneak its way into the playoffs. With Trey Yesavage and Shane Bieber already on the IL, the rotation has begun leaking oil, and that’s not something this power-starved lineup is equipped to handle. The Jays still have a path to the final Wild Card spot, but it’s becoming an increasingly tenuous one, and it’s hard to see them making much noise even if they did get in.
–CL
15. Houston Astros
Getting swept at home by the Braves this weekend might well wind up costing the Astros a playoff spot. The closing schedule isn’t too tough, with trips to Seattle and Sacramento on tap. Still, if Houston doesn’t figure out where its high-powered offense went before it’s too late — and if Joe Espada can’t stop his bullpen from blowing late leads — Yordan Alvarez’s MVP season may well be for nought. As it stands, this looks like a team with fatal flaws that will spoil what could have been a deep run in a wide-open AL.
–CL
14. Chicago White Sox
Reality hit the White Sox real quick. Chicago has lingered around .500 for longer than they'd care to admit, and it was only a matter of time before the rest of the Central caught up to them. Munetaka Murakami has been dreadful since the trade deadline, and thus any contract extension talks have been put on hold. If the White Sox can hold on to a playoff spot, they'll be one of the best stories in October. If not, this season could all be for naught.
-MP
13. Texas Rangers
All of a sudden, the Rangers find themselves back in control of the AL West and home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs. Of course, that says more about the West than it does about Texas; this is still a .500 team, one without a ton of depth on either side of the ball. The interesting thing, though, is that this lineup has finally started to show signs of life of late. Take care of business against the Twins and Mets this week, and no one’s going to want to face a team with Jacob deGrom and Nathan Eovaldi in the rotation plus an offense featuring Corey Seager, Wyatt Langford and Josh Jung.
-CL
12. Pittsburgh Pirates
The narrative Pirates fans are spinning these days is the same web every National League non-playoff team will get caught in this week; if only we played in the American League! Yes, the disparity between leagues is easy to blame for the Pirates shortcomings, but the front office also fell short in acquiring bullpen arms last winter, which could've kept Pittsburgh from blowing an extraordinary number of leads in the season's first half. That'll haunt these Pirates forever.
-MP
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
It's not Arizona's fault that their primary competition for a Wild Card spot, San Diego, has become one of the hottest teams in baseball over the last few weeks. Either way, though, Arizona has simply run out of bullets, especially in a rotation that hasn't gotten the boost from Corbin Burnes' return that they were hoping for. Eduardo Rodriguez has turned back into a pumpkin, and there's just not enough depth to keep pace with what's become a beast of an NL playoff chase.
–CL
10. Cleveland Guardians
Here we go again with the Guardians. Cleveland is a legitimate threat in a weak American League. Much like last season, the Guards are taking advantage of a fellow contender floundering down the stretch. This is when Cleveland plays its best baseball, so it should be no surprise they've won five straight games heading into Monday's potential postseason preview against the Red Sox.
-MP
9. Boston Red Sox
Dropping consecutive series to the Rangers and Rays won’t do much to Boston’s postseason outlook — they’ve been more or less locked into a Wild Card series in the Bronx for a while now — but it still doesn’t inspire confidence in this team’s ability to make a run come October. This offense is once again mired in a power outage, and while getting Willson Contreras and others back from the IL figures to help, who knows when that might actually be. And there’s still just a real dearth of power here that even this pitching staff might not be able to make up for.
–CL
8. Philadelphia Phillies
I don’t know what to think of the Philadelphia Phillies. On one hand, a rotation led by Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sanchez, a healthy Jesus Luzardo, a rejuvenated Aaron Nola and a much-improved Andrew Painter should will them to wins. On the other hand, Luzardo is not healthy, the lineup is top-heavy and the bullpen, outside of Jhoan Duran, is an utter disaster. The Phillies are almost certainly going to make the playoffs, but their losses in New York this week ruined any last hope they had at a division title. And with how they’re playing right now, I don’t know if I’d pick them to get beyond the Wild Card Round.
–ZR
7. Chicago Cubs
The Cubs playoff parade was put on hold Sunday as Alex Bregman was struck in the face by a foul ball. Bregman was taken to the local hospital, and it's unclear how much time he will miss as of this writing. Chicago's postseason hopes may hang in the balance, as their one clear advantage over every other NL team is their lineup. The Cubs have scored the most runs in baseball this year.
-MP
6. San Diego Padres
Yes, the schedule has helped, particularly series against Miami, Colorado, Washington, San Francisco and Cincinnati. But no matter who they've played, the Padres look like a different team from the one we saw for much of the year, with their big bats finally mashing and their rotation coming into focus with Nick Pivetta now back in the fold. San Diego is now dead even with Chicago and Philly in the Wild Card race, and no one will want to face this lineup and this bullpen in a short series.
–CL
5. New York Yankees
Just when it seemed like New York was getting ready to make a move, with Aaron Judge finally back in the lineup after months on the shelf, the reigning AL MVP landed right back on the IL — this time with a calf strain that could well jeopardize his entire postseason. It’s been that sort of year for the Yankees, which have the pitching to keep believing in them as contenders but just haven’t been able to put it all together enough to take command of their own playoff destiny. And with a Judge-less offense and a penchant for mistake-filled baseball, winning three series in a row feels like a tough ask even in this AL.
–CL
4. Atlanta Braves
The Atlanta Braves punched their ticket to the playoffs this week, and thanks to the Phillies’ struggles, they’re on the cusp of winning the NL East — ensuring a top-three seed in the National League. Tyler Mahle pitched another gem, and Ronald Acuña Jr. is hitting his stride at the perfect time. There’re still some concerns with the team, like the No. 3 spot in their rotation and struggling stars like Austin Riley and Ozzie Albies, but getting to the playoffs is a big deal, and the Braves can take pride in checking that box.
–ZR
3. Tampa Bay Rays
The Rays may well have sewn up the AL East this week, taking two of three from the Red Sox over the weekend to stretch their lead over the Yankees ahead of an all-important four-game set in the Bronx beginning on Tuesday. Even if New York were to sweep all four, though, Tampa would still have the inside track to the division and the No. 1 overall seed. This pitching staff continues to thrive beyond all expectation even with some recent injuries, and the hitting has done just enough. Whether that recipe will withstand the postseason is the only question now.
–CL
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Don't look now, but L.A.'s lineup has begun to stir, with Kyle Tucker looking like the player the Dodgers thought they were paying for this offseason. They also got Edwin Diaz back this week, and he's suddenly looking like the star closer of old — potentially answering this team's biggest question entering October. We know the rotation will be there; if they have Tucker at the height of his powers and a one-two punch in Diaz and Tanner Scott at the end of games, the three-peat march might be back on.
–CL
1. Milwaukee Brewers
The Brewers set a franchise record with 98 wins on Sunday. They still have a full week to go to add to that mark, and appear likely to reach the 100-win plateau. That's a great accomplishment, but it won't mean squat if Milwaukee falls to the Los Angeles Dodgers — or any other NL team for that matter — on their way to that elusive NL pennant. The Brewers are the favorites, but the Dodgers are lingering right behind them.
-MP

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers beat the San Francisco Giants, 3-1, on Sunday and improved to 96-60 on the year. They completed the series sweep of the divisional rivals and notched their fourth-straight win (and 14th of the last 17).
After Jack Dreyer took the start and allowed an earned run in the first inning, Emmet Sheehan pitched the next 5.1 frames and stole the show on the mound. He struck out nine, allowed one hit, one walk and no earned runs.
Offensively, Teoscar Hernndez, Freddie Freeman, Max Muncy and Josue De Paula each had a two-hit game. De Paula was 5-for-10 over the course of the series, just the first of hopefully many more at Dodger Stadium.
Ahead of the eventual victory, southpaw Tarik Skubal unfortunately had to be placed on the bereavement list. As he deals with his personal matter, it is likely that he will still make one more start (he is next scheduled for Sept. 26) before the postseason.
In other news, manager Dave Roberts made a somewhat surprising admission regarding superstar Mookie Betts. After hitting just .235 before the All-Star break, Betts has completely turned things around and looks like a more familiar version of himself, hitting .322 in his last 30 games.
"I couldn't tell you that I saw this," Roberts said on Saturday regarding Betts' turnaround. "But I just felt that he was stronger. He's worked hard on that. He looks great. He's not going to stop working, and just for it to come together has been great."
Finally, a Dodgers pitcher was demoted as part of the four-player roster move made on Sunday. The right-hander has an impressive 1.32 ERA across 26 games (27.1 innings) at the Triple-A level, but in 11 appearances with the Dodgers this season, he has an 8.10 ERA across 10 innings of work.

item.title: [purplerow.com] Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
item.dc:creator: James Riggenbach
item.description: The Colorado Rockies are 57–99. Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take? One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball. item.content:encoded:
The Colorado Rockies are 57–99.
Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take?
One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball.
These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out.
The team with the worst record in baseball gets to steal one player from a playoff team.
There are, naturally, some restrictions. We’re freezing the playoff field as it stood before games on Sunday, September 20. The player has to come from one of those 12 teams, cannot be a pending free agent, and you cannot take the player who leads his team in FanGraphs WAR. The Rockies also inherit the player’s existing contract.
No, one player is not suddenly turning the Rockies into a contender. But could one poached superstar at least keep this thing from becoming five consecutive 100-loss seasons?
Here’s the board:
| Team | Off limits: fWAR leader | Highest available fWAR | Other players worth considering |
| Rays | Junior Caminero (5.2) | Drew Rasmussen (4.7) | Jonathan Aranda (3) |
| Guardians | Parker Messick (4.6) | Steven Kwan (3.4) | Gavin Williams (3.4), Brayan Rocchio (3.3), José Ramírez (2.2) |
| Rangers | Ezequiel Duran (4.6) | Jacob deGrom (4.2) | Josh Jung (2.9), Wyatt Langford (2.8) |
| Yankees | Cam Schlittler (6.1) | Ben Rice (4) | Cody Bellinger (3.9), Aaron Judge (2) |
| Red Sox | Willson Contreras (4.1) | Payton Tolle (4) | Ceddanne Rafaela (3.9), Ranger Suárez (3.7) |
| White Sox | Miguel Vargas (5) | Chase Meidroth (4) | Tristan Peters (3.9), Sean Burke (3.1) |
| Brewers | Jacob Misiorowski (6.3) | Brice Turang (5.4) | Jackson Chourio (4), Jake Bauers (3.6) |
| Dodgers | Shohei Ohtani (6.7) | Yoshinobu Yamamoto (4.7) | Max Muncy (4.3), Andy Pages (3.9) |
| Braves | Chris Sale (5.7) | Michael Harris II (4) | Matt Olson (4), Drake Baldwin (3.1) |
| Cubs | Pete Crow-Armstrong (10.2) | Alex Bregman (5) | Dansby Swanson (3.6) |
| Padres | Fernando Tatis Jr. (5) | Jackson Merrill (4) | Ty France (3.8), Mason Miller (3.7) |
| Phillies | Cristopher Sánchez (5.8) | Jesús Luzardo (5.6) | Zack Wheeler (3.5), Bryce Harper (3.4) |
For me, the choice comes down to Brice Turang, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Aaron Judge.
Turang is probably the sensible choice.
At 5.4 fWAR, he would easily lead the Rockies, giving them a legitimate top-end player while immediately solving second base for the foreseeable future. He’s 26, hitting .266/.367/.441 with an .808 OPS, and brings value on both sides of the ball with elite range, strong baserunning and a 95th-percentile walk rate.
It would be a very easy way to make the roster better.
But the Rockies really need starting pitching.
Enter Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He’s 14–8 with a 2.51 ERA, 178 strikeouts and a 0.87 WHIP over 179 innings. His Statcast profile is just as impressive: 100th-percentile pitching run value, 99th-percentile fastball run value, 95th-percentile offspeed run value and a 91st-percentile xERA.
Pitchers are risky, and Yamamoto comes with a lot of money attached. But it’s hard to argue with either the profile or the results, and the addition of the Penner family makes absorbing that contract a lot easier to imagine.
Speaking of high-priced items...
Aaron Judge.
Judge being available is basically a loophole created by our own stupid rule. Injuries have limited him to just 285 plate appearances, which is why he sits at only 2 fWAR, but he’s still hitting .241/.360/.511 with 15 home runs.
And the underlying numbers are still very much Judge: a .396 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 57.5% hard-hit rate.
It is very hard to look at that and say, “No thanks.”
After all, Aaron Judge is the type of hitter that, if he were playing 81 games a year at Coors Field, I might take out a small loan for season tickets.
So who are you stealing?

item.title: [sbsun.com] Emmet Sheehan strengthens postseason case as Dodgers sweep Giants
item.dc:creator: Bill Plunkett
item.description: LOS ANGELES — Hiding behind that 5.00 ERA Emmet Sheehan toted around for much of the season might have been a valuable postseason piece. Sheehan allowed just one hit in 5⅓ scoreless innings on Sunday afternoon as the Dodgers beat the San Francisco Giants, 3-1, to complete a three-game sweep. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Hiding behind that 5.00 ERA Emmet Sheehan toted around for much of the season might have been a valuable postseason piece.
Sheehan allowed just one hit in 5⅓ scoreless innings on Sunday afternoon as the Dodgers beat the San Francisco Giants, 3-1, to complete a three-game sweep.
Sheehan retired 16 of the 18 batters he faced, allowing just one single and walking one while striking out nine.
“I’ve loved the version we’ve seen of Emmet the last three outings,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “He’s been fantastic.
“We’ve seen confidence. We’ve seen when you’re essentially fighting for your life to create an opportunity for yourself. That’s what I see. There’s urgency. I like the way that he’s trusting his stuff. He’s in a good spot physically, and you know the performance has been fantastic.”
The outing was Sheehan’s third consecutive outstanding performance this month as he has bounced between Triple-A and the majors. It cemented a spot in the Dodgers’ postseason bullpen after a rough season for the 26-year-old right-hander – an outcome that did not seem likely when he was demoted to Triple-A in early August.
“I don’t know that I proved anything to myself. It was just getting a couple things right and I think I’m in a much better spot now,” Sheehan said.
“My confidence stayed the same the whole time. I knew the coaches down there were going to help me and I was going to get right. I took that approach going into it. I wasn’t helping the team here so I needed that a little bit.”
Sheehan has been called up for two starts this month and pitched in ‘bulk’ following Jack Dreyer as an opener on Sunday. Sheehan carried a 5.29 ERA into September after 20 starts for the Dodgers that landed him back in the minors.
In his three September outings, though, Sheehan has shown rediscovered fastball command after working on his delivery in Triple-A. He has allowed just one run in 17 innings, holding hitters to a .105 average (6 for 57) with 24 strikeouts and three walks. After giving up 20 home runs in those first 20 starts, he has allowed just one in his 17 September innings.
If his confidence didn’t need repair, his delivery and pitch mix needed some work.
Now two years removed from Tommy John surgery, Sheehan was thrown by not quite having recovered all of his fastball velocity this year. When he chased those extra miles per hour, it was counterproductive. He has become more comfortable at 94-95 mph now.
“I think it’s a few things,” he said Sunday. “Definitely … being more comfortable in my delivery, being out there staying free and easy with everything, not trying to do too much. Instead of saying, ‘I need 97 here.’ It’s more like ‘If I hit my spot, he’s not going to hit it.’”
They haven’t. Sheehan has gotten 50 swings-and-misses in his three outings this month, nearly half of them (24) on his reborn four-seam fastball. He also got six on his curveball on Sunday.
“That’s something that (assistant pitching coach) Connor (McGuinness), (pitching coach) Mark (Prior) and I and the coaches down in Triple-A have been working on is just expanding the front-to-back game with the fastball and the curveball,” Sheehan said. “I think some guys ended up throughout the season sitting mid-speed, slider-changeup, on me. Having that change of speeds the last couple has been very important.”
The Dodgers moved Sheehan to the bullpen for the postseason last October and saw him as a big weapon in that role. The results were mixed, however, in part because of some pitch tipping issues which Sheehan said have been addressed. He will be wiser this time around, he said.
“Definitely,” Sheehan said. “I think the routine of everything can be a little bit hard to adjust to right away. So having that experience helps a lot. Just getting back into that, I know what I need to do to get ready to go into the game.”
The Dodgers gave him a little bit of a test drive by using Dreyer as an ‘opener’ before him. The Giants scratched out one run in the first inning against Dreyer when he walked leadoff man Jonah Cox. Cox moved to second base on a wild pickoff attempt by Dreyer, stole third and scored on Victor Bericoto’s RBI single. The Giants had just one more hit in the game.
“I think that obviously there’s a 97 that plays better, but 94-95 commanded still misses bats,” Roberts said of Sheehan, who will rejoin Oklahoma City for the Triple-A playoffs this week before returning to the Dodgers for the postseason. “That’s one part of it. The other part of it is holding the velocity. And so, for me, the last three or four since he’s been back here, he’s held those 94s and 95s for the, call it 85 pitches.”
The Giants’ run against Dreyer stood up as the only run of the day until Tommy Edman emerged from a 2-for-41 slump to hit a solo home run in the sixth inning.
The Dodgers broke the 1-1 tie in the seventh on singles by Max Muncy and Josue De Paula followed by an RBI double from Kiké Hernandez.
They stranded De Paula and Hernandez in scoring position, but singles by Teoscar Hernandez, Freddie Freeman and Muncy produced another run in the eighth inning.
Kris Bubic, Brock Stewart and Tanner Scott combined on 2⅔ innings of hitless relief to close out the combined two-hitter for the Dodgers’ 96th win. With the win, the Dodgers’ magic number to clinch a first-round bye over the Atlanta Braves (who clinched the National League East division title on Sunday) dropped to three with six games left in the regular season.
The Dodgers (96-60) remain two games behind the Milwaukee Brewers (98-58) for the top seed, though the Brewers also hold the head-to-head tiebreaker. The No. 3 seed – currently Atlanta (92-64) – will play host to a best-of-three Wild Card Series against either the Chicago Cubs (87-69), San Diego Padres (87-69) or Philadelphia Phillies (86-70).

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers considering Emmet Sheehan for playoff role after gem in win over Giants
item.dc:creator: Dylan Hernandez
item.description: Emmet Sheehan’s next start will be in the minor leagues. The right-hander might be out of sight, but that doesn’t mean he will be out of mind. His scheduled start Saturday for triple-A Oklahoma City in a Pacific Coast League playoff game is part of a design to prepare him to pitch for the Dodgers in October. item.content:encoded:
Emmet Sheehan’s next start will be in the minor leagues.
The right-hander might be out of sight, but that doesn’t mean he will be out of mind.
His scheduled start Saturday for triple-A Oklahoma City in a Pacific Coast League playoff game is part of a design to prepare him to pitch for the Dodgers in October.
Sheehan has pitched his way into consideration for a spot on the playoff roster.
His quote-unquote demotion came after he pitched 5 ⅓ scoreless innings in the Los Angeles Dodgers’ sweep-sealing 3–1 victory over the San Francisco Giants Sunday.
The game was the third Sheehan pitched this month for the Dodgers. His numbers in those three games: 17 innings pitched, one run allowed, 24 strikeouts, three walks.
“I’ve loved the version we’ve seen of Emmet the last three outings,” manager Dave Roberts said. “He’s been fantastic.”
Sent down to Oklahoma City in early August, Sheehan returned to the major leagues earlier this month with a slightly modified arsenal that has significantly improved his results. He’s thrown his curveball more, and his increased inability to change speeds has made his fastball play up even when he’s not touching 97 mph with it.
“I think that obviously there’s a 97 that plays better, but 94–95 commanded still misses bats,” Roberts said. “So I think that’s something that, that’s one part of it. The other part of it is holding the velocity. And so, for me, the last three or four since he’s been back here, he’s held those 94s and 95s for the, call it, 85 pitches.”
With the Dodgers expecting to start Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal and Tyler Glasnow in the postseason, the team has started the process of moving Sheehan into a relief role by having Jack Dreyer pitch an inning as opener Sunday. Sheehan was down in triple-A over the last week but a roster spot for him was opened up because Skubal went on the bereavement list.
Sheehan entered the game in the second inning and pitched into the seventh. He gave up only one hit and one walk; he struck out nine.
He said he has made it a point to feel “free and easy” with his delivery.
“Instead of saying, ‘I need 97 [mph] here,’ it’s more like, ‘If I hit my spot, he’s not going to hit it,’” Sheehan said.
What it means
The teams with the two-best records in each league will earn a first-round bye and the Dodgers are close to wrapping up one of those spots. With their win over the Giants, the Dodgers maintained a four-game lead over the Atlanta Braves for the National League’s No. 2 seed. Both teams have only six games remaining in the regular season.
Who’s hot
Left-hander Kris Bubic, who was acquired from the Kansas City Royals at the trade deadline, replaced Sheehan in the seventh inning and registered the final two outs of the inning. Bubic struck out Scott Bandura, only for Shay Whitcomb to reach base on a throwing error by Max Muncy.
No problem: Bubic forced Grant McCray to fly out to left field.
Bubic has pitched 2 ⅔ innings in three appearances for the Dodgers over the last week, and he still hasn’t allowed a run. He has struck out four.
Roberts said he’s also pitched his way into consideration for a spot on the playoff roster.
“It’s nothing overpowering, but there’s just funky swings, soft contact,” Roberts said. “I see him as a neutral pitcher, gets left and right out, and I like those converted starters because he knows how to navigate lineups.”
Who’s Not
For today, this section should be renamed “Who Wasn’t Hot.”
The label certainly applied to Tommy Edman, who was two for his last 42 before his sixth-inning at-bat: That’s when Edman jumped on an inside cutter from Carson Seymour and launched it into the visiting bullpen behind the right-field wall.
Edman’s home run tied the game at 1–1.
Up next
The Dodgers have a day off Monday. They will resume play Tuesday when they host the San Diego Padres, who will send No. 1 starter Michael King (12-9, 3.03 ERA) to the mound. The Dodgers won’t have a traditional starter, as Roberts said the team is planning for a bullpen game.

item.content:encoded:
Por DAN GREENSPAN
LOS ÁNGELES (AP) — Kiké Hernández conectó un doble productor que puso a su equipo por delante en la séptima entrada, Emmet Sheehan no permitió carreras en 5 1/3 innings, y los Dodgers de Los Ángeles vencieron 3-1 a los Gigantes de San Francisco el domingo para completar una barrida de tres juegos.
El boricua Hernández atacó el primer lanzamiento que vio de Sam Hentges (1-7) e impulsó a Max Muncy para poner a los Dodgers arriba 2-1. Muncy añadió una carrera de seguridad con un sencillo en la octava.
Kris Bubic (4-2) lanzó 2/3 de inning para llevarse la victoria, y Tanner Scott se encargó de la novena entrada para su 23er salvamento.
Sheehan aprovechó al máximo un juego de bullpen para reforzar sus credenciales de cara a integrar el roster de postemporada de los Dodgers como relevista largo. Ponchó a nueve, permitió un hit y otorgó una base por bolas después de relevar a Jack Dreyer en la segunda entrada.
Matt Wilkinson permitió tres hits y no dio bases por bolas, además de ponchar a seis en cinco episodios sin permitir carreras, pero el bullpen de los Gigantes se vino abajo. El zurdo de 23 años fue adquirido como parte del canje que envió al receptor Patrick Bailey a Cleveland en mayo.
Tommy Edman conectó un jonrón hacia el jardín derecho en la sexta entrada para empatar el juego 1-1, castigando al relevista Carson Seymour con un batazo de 400 pies.
Jonah Cox recibió una base por bolas abriendo la entrada para ayudar a que los Gigantes tomaran ventaja 1-0. Cox llegó a segunda por un mal intento de sorprenderlo en la inicial por parte de Dreyer antes de robarse la tercera, y un sencillo de Victor Bericoto lo remolcó.
___

item.title: [bignewsnetwork.com] Emmet Sheehan dominates Giants in long relief as Dodgers cap sweep
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.description: Emmet Sheehan dominates Giants in long relief as Dodgers cap sweep (Photo credit: William Liang) Emmet Sheehan pitched brilliantly in long relief, Enrique Hernandez broke a seventh-inning tie with a run-scoring double and the Los Angeles Dodgers completed a three-game home sweep of the rival San Francisco Giants with a 3-1 victory Sunday afternoon. Tommy Edman homered for Los Angeles (96-60), which won its fourth straight and remained four games ahead of the Atlanta Braves (92-64) in the race fo
item.content:encoded:
Emmet Sheehan dominates Giants in long relief as Dodgers cap sweep
(Photo credit: William Liang)
Emmet Sheehan pitched brilliantly in long relief, Enrique Hernandez broke a seventh-inning tie with a run-scoring double and the Los Angeles Dodgers completed a three-game home sweep of the rival San Francisco Giants with a 3-1 victory Sunday afternoon.
Tommy Edman homered for Los Angeles (96-60), which won its fourth straight and remained four games ahead of the Atlanta Braves (92-64) in the race for the National League's No. 2 seed and a first-round bye in the playoffs.
After Victor Bericoto had singled home Jonah Cox in the first inning against Dodgers opener Jack Dreyer, Sheehan took over to start the second and held the Giants to just one hit over the next 5 1/3 scoreless innings. Nine of the 16 outs he recorded came via strikeout.
Meanwhile, Edman's homer, his seventh of the season, produced a 1-1 tie in the sixth. It came off Giants reliever Carson Seymour, who had replaced Matt Wilkinson after five shutout innings.
Making his fifth career start, Wilkinson limited the Dodgers to three hits while striking out six.
The clubs took the 1-1 tie into the bottom of the seventh, when one-out singles by Max Muncy and Josue De Paula off Sam Hentges (1-7) set the stage for Hernandez, whose double to center field drove in the go-ahead run.
Muncy provided an insurance run with an RBI single in the eighth that scored Teoscar Hernandez, who had singled.
Kris Bubic (4-2), Brock Stewart and Tanner Scott threw the final 2 2/3 innings for the Dodgers, allowing just two baserunners, one on an error and the other via a walk.
Scott walked Brett Harris with two outs in the ninth, bringing the potential tying run to the plate. But the left-hander locked down his 23rd save by striking out Osleivis Basabe.
Muncy, De Paula, Teoscar Hernandez and Freddie Freeman had two hits apiece for the Dodgers, who will host the second-place San Diego Padres for three games before closing the regular season with three in San Francisco beginning Friday.
Jung Hoo Lee joined Bericoto with the only hits for the Giants (64-92), who completed their road schedule with a 28-53 record.
--Field Level Media

But Dodgers manager Dave Roberts appeared to believe that Skubal will be back by Friday, telling reporters he would miss "a
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers placed pitcher Tarik Skubal on the bereavement list on Sunday, which means he could miss his final regular-season turn in the rotation next week.
Skubal's next start is scheduled for Friday against the San Francisco Giants, which could fall within the three-to-seven days that players are allowed to be away from the team while on the bereavement list. But Dodgers manager Dave Roberts appeared to believe that Skubal will be back by Friday, telling reporters he would miss "a couple days."
"Some personal stuff going on, but he's fine," Roberts said, via MLB.com's Sonja Chen.
Skubal pitched in Saturday's 10-4 win over the Giants, allowing four runs and eight hits over five innings. He walked two batters with three strikeouts, tying his lowest total of the season. Saturday's game was the first time Skubal gave up more than three runs in his nine starts with the Dodgers. according to The Athletic's Fabian Ardaya.
Tarik Skubal pitched five innings and allowed four runs but is grateful for the offensive support.
“Yeah, no doubt. Obviously, I wasn't very good today, but the offense and defense and bullpen picked me up big time, and that's what good teams do,” Skubal said. “You know, they… pic.twitter.com/4TUdrQqgH8
"Obviously, I wasn't very good today, but the offense and defense and bullpen picked me up big time, and that's what good teams do," Skubal said after the game.
In his nine starts with the Dodgers since being acquired from the Detroit Tigers before the MLB trade deadline, Skubal has a 2.95 ERA and 4-2 record with 60 strikeouts in 55 innings.
The Dodgers took a 2-0 lead on a first-inning RBI double by Max Muncy and Mookie Betts hitting a run-scoring single in the second. But San Francisco tied the score in the third on a 2-run homer from Victor Bericoto, hitting a fastball left in the very middle of the strike zone by Skubal.
The two teams then traded runs during the third through fifth innings, resulting in a 4-4 tie, before the Dodgers pulled away on a 2-run hit by Tommy Edman and RBI single from Miguel Rojas. In the following inning, the Dodgers added three more runs with Will Smith driving in a run and Josue De Paula hitting a 2-run single.
To fill Skubal's spot on the active roster, Emmet Sheehan was recalled from Triple-A Oklahoma City. He pitched 5 1/3 scoreless innings with one hit allowed and nine strikeouts, taking over for opener Jack Dreyer in the Dodgers' 3-1 win. In his previous two starts before being optioned, Sheehan allowed one run over 11 2/3 innings with 15 strikeouts.

item.title: [Newsday] Dodgers get better of Giants' bullpen in 3-1 win to sweep three-game series
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.description: LOS ANGELES — Kiké Hernández hit a go-ahead RBI double in the seventh inning, Emmet Sheehan did not give up a run in 5 1/3 innings, and the Los Angeles Dodgers beat the San Francisco Giants 3-1 on Sunday to complete a three-game sweep. Hernández jumped on the first pitch he saw from Sam Hentges (1-7), driving in Max Muncy to put the Dodgers ahead 2-1. Muncy pushed an insurance run across with a single in the eighth. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Kiké Hernández hit a go-ahead RBI double in the seventh inning, Emmet Sheehan did not give up a run in 5 1/3 innings, and the Los Angeles Dodgers beat the San Francisco Giants 3-1 on Sunday to complete a three-game sweep.
Hernández jumped on the first pitch he saw from Sam Hentges (1-7), driving in Max Muncy to put the Dodgers ahead 2-1. Muncy pushed an insurance run across with a single in the eighth.
Kris Bubic (4-2) pitched 2/3 of an inning for the win, and Tanner Scott handled the ninth inning for his 23rd save.
Sheehan made the most of a bullpen game to strengthen his credentials for making the Dodgers’ postseason roster as a long reliever. He had nine strikeouts against one hit and one walk after taking over from Jack Dreyer in the second inning.
Matt Wilkinson allowed three hits and no walks while striking out six in five scoreless innings, but the Giants’ bullpen buckled. The 23-year-old left-hander was acquired as part of the trade that sent catcher Patrick Bailey to Cleveland in May.
Tommy Edman homered to right in the sixth inning to tie the game at 1, tagging reliever Carson Seymour for the 400-foot shot.
Jonah Cox drew a leadoff walk to help spot the Giants their 1-0 lead. Cox reached second on a bad pickoff attempt by Dreyer before stealing third, and Victor Bericoto’s single drove him home.
Up next
Giants: RHP Blade Tidwell (1-2, 4.56 ERA) starts in the opener of a three-game series against the Minnesota Twins on Monday night, facing RHP Bailey Ober (7-6, 4.32).
Dodgers: Manager Dave Roberts said there would be another bullpen game Tuesday night to start a three-game series against the San Diego Padres, who have yet to set their rotation.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Is it still a rivalry? Dodgers complete sweep of woeful Giants
item.dc:creator: Kevin Baxter
item.description: Is it still a rivalry? Dodgers complete sweep of woeful Giants - Click here to listen to this article - Only the Pirates and Cubs have met more often than the Dodgers and Giants, who faced off for the first time in 1889. And over all that time, the Dodgers are just two games better, with 1,294 wins to the Giants’ 1,292. The Dodgers and Giants have also won more pennants, made more World Series appearances and have more players wearing their caps in the Hall of Fame than any other National
item.content:encoded:
Is it still a rivalry? Dodgers complete sweep of woeful Giants
- Click here to listen to this article
-
Only the Pirates and Cubs have met more often than the Dodgers and Giants, who faced off for the first time in 1889. And over all that time, the Dodgers are just two games better, with 1,294 wins to the Giants’ 1,292.
The Dodgers and Giants have also won more pennants, made more World Series appearances and have more players wearing their caps in the Hall of Fame than any other National League teams, all of which fueled a rivalry that was once among the most visceral and passionate in American sports.
But that was then and this is now.
After Sunday’s 3-1 victory over the Giants, the Dodgers’ 14th win in their last 17 games, the team could finish a season with 100 wins for the fourth time in six years. The Giants have had just one winning record in that time.
The Dodgers (96-60), who have won five straight division titles, are headed to the postseason for a record-tying 14th consecutive year. The Giants will miss the playoffs for a fifth straight season.
So is the rivalry dead? That depends on who you ask.
“It’s always a rivalry,” Giants pitcher Logan Webb. “We’d like to make it a little closer when it comes to the standings. But I definitely feel it when I throw against them.”
But then Webb, who is from Northern California, grew up with the rivalry and, as the longest-tenured Giant, pitched against the Dodgers in games that mattered. Giants coach Ron Washington, who made his major league debut with the Dodgers when the rivalry was still a thing, said many players on San Francisco’s roster don’t know that background.
Mookie Betts hits three doubles and the Dodgers piled up 15 hits in a 10-4 win over the San Francisco Giants with Shohei Ohtani’s return on the horizon.
“It should be a rivalry. But I don’t think the young kids we got know anything about a rivalry. They’re not history buffs.”
Webb said it’s the responsibility of the veterans on both sides to keep that history alive by explaining the enmity to the young players.
“I think there are still guys that came up in the system that know what it’s like,” he said. “It’s my job to kind of hype these guys up to play a game like this.”
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, who played for the Dodgers and Giants during his 10-year career, agrees the rivalry now exists more in the history books than the current standings, where the Giants have been overtaken by the San Diego Padres, who will finish second to the Dodgers in the N.L. West for the fourth time in five seasons.
“It’s certainly a rivalry in the sense of the history, the fan bases,” Roberts said. “But obviously it’s about relevancy. The Padres have been successful the last handful of years, and so it’s certainly built some momentum. The geography lends itself to that too.
“But Dodgers Giants is always fun.”
It hasn’t been so much fun for the Giants lately. San Francisco hasn’t won the season series with the Dodgers since 2021 and has lost more than 90 games this year for the first time in nine seasons.
On Sunday they went in front three batters into the game with Johan Cox working Dodger opener Jack Dreyer for a leadoff walk, then making his way around the bases on Dreyer’s throwing error, a stolen base and a one-one single by Victor Bericoto.
But San Francisco didn’t get another hit until Jung Hoo Lee singled with one out in the sixth.
That allowed the Dodgers to tie the score in the sixth on Tommy Edman’s seventh home run of the season just inside the right-field foul pole. An inning later they went ahead to stay when Max Muncy singled under a sliding Cox at second, moved to third on a single by rookie Josue De Paula and scored on Kiké Hernández’s double to center.
A two-out single by Muncy, his second of the game, scored Teoscar Hernández, who also had two hits, in the eighth inning with the final run.
Even the slumping Freddie Freeman contributed to the Dodgers’ 11-hit attack, ending an 0-for-11 slide with a broken-bat single in the fourth then singling again in the eighth.
Sunday’s result helped clarify the Dodgers’ once-muddy playoff picture. With six games left in the regular season, the Dodgers lead Atlanta by four games in the race for the second seed in the National League playoffs, which would give them a first-round bye and the homefield advantage in the division series.
The team’s postseason roster may be getting clearer as well. Right-hander Emmet Sheehan, who made 22 starts this season, came out of the bullpen for the first time Sunday and was brilliant in his audition for the playoffs.
“If there is a role in the postseason, it will be out of the [bull]pen,” Roberts said of Sheehan, who gave up just a hit and walk, striking out nine — one off his season high — in 5 1/3 innings.
Tyler Glasnow hasn’t had the greatest of seasons, but the Dodgers will need him to deliver in the playoffs if they want to win another World Series title.
De Paula, meanwhile, who also doubled in running his modest hitting streak to four games, appears to have secured a job as the team’s left-handed bat off the bench while utility player Hyeseong Kim, who has spent the last four months in the minors, will rejoin the Dodgers after the triple-A playoffs and be considered for a roster spot as a pinch-runner and late-inning defensive replacement.
“My expectation is that Hyeseong will be here during the off week and potentially be a conversation for the postseason because he has the ability to run, play defense, and steal a base,” Roberts said.
After Monday’s off day, the final break of the regular season for the Dodgers, the team is expected to activate Andy Pages, Roki Sasaki and Shohei Ohtani from the injured list during its three-game series with the Padres.
